cse-2014-1-cs-36.approach: Read the language off the DFA first: every input ends in the accepting state exactly when the last symbol is 1. Then test each expression against that language, looking for a string ending in 1 that it misses.

steps.title: Language of the DFA
steps.body: On 1 the DFA always goes to the accepting state (from start, and by the self-loop on the accepting state); on 0 it always goes to the start state. So the state after reading $w$ depends only on the **last symbol**: $L = \{w : w \text{ ends in } 1\} = (0+1)^*1$.

scene.caption: Any 1 leads to the accepting state; any 0 leads back to start.

steps.title: Check I: 0*1(1+00*1)*
steps.body: $0^*1$ reads up to the first 1. After that the remainder of a string ending in 1 splits into blocks, each block being a lone $1$ or a run of zeros followed by 1, i.e. $00^*1$. So $0^*1(1+00^*1)^*$ generates exactly the strings ending in 1. **I is correct.**

steps.title: Check II: 0*1*1+11*0*1
steps.body: Every string of $0^*1^*1$ or $11^*0^*1$ ends in 1, but the string $10101$ (ends in 1, accepted by the DFA) has the shape 1-0-1-0-1, which fits neither $0^*1^*1$ (no 0 after a 1) nor $11^*0^*1$ (only one 0-run). Even $0101$ is missed. **II is wrong.**

scene.caption: Trace 10101: it ends in the accepting state, but II cannot generate it.

steps.title: Check III and conclude
steps.body: $(0+1)^*1$ is literally "any string, then a 1" = $L$. **III is correct.** Hence I and III only.

optionAnalysis.reason: II is not equivalent: it misses strings such as 0101 and 10101.
I and III both describe exactly the strings ending in 1.
II is wrong, and I is correct, so this pairing fails twice.
II does not generate all strings ending in 1.

pitfalls: Checking only that each expression generates strings ending in 1 (soundness) and forgetting completeness — II is sound but incomplete.
cse-2014-1-cs-36.verification: Traced 0101 and 10101 through the DFA (both accepted) and confirmed neither matches either branch of II, while both match I as 0*1 · (00*1) · (00*1) style splits.

steps.title: Consequence of a poly-time clique algorithm
steps.body: CLIQUE (decision form) is NP-complete. Computing the largest clique in polynomial time decides CLIQUE in polynomial time, so an NP-complete problem is in P $\Rightarrow$ $P = NP$.

steps.title: Where NPC sits
steps.body: If $P = NP$, any language $L \in NP$ with $L \ne \emptyset, \Sigma^*$ is NP-complete (reduce by solving the instance in poly time and outputting a fixed yes/no instance of $L$). But $\emptyset$ and $\Sigma^*$ have no yes/no instance to map to, so they are **not** NP-complete. Hence $NPC \subsetneq P = NP$ — diagram (C).
